answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Top-level resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (resource type name: databaseAccounts).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create a MongoDB API account: az cosmosdb create -n my-docdb -g my-rg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2. This is in the core az CLI (az cosmosdb).

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (AzureRM): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (resource type name in HCL: azurerm_cosmosdb_account).

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical connection string for the MongoDB-compatible Azure DocumentDB/Cosmos account: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. You can also get an SRV URI: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/<dbname>?ssl=true. Username is often in the form <dbuser>@<account> and TLS/SSL must be enabled.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is usually billed in Request Units (RUs) for Cosmos DB accounts (provisioned RU/s or autoscale RU/s); there is also a serverless option for some accounts. (Note: some managed MongoDB offerings or dedicated SKUs may expose vCore-like tiers, but the default Cosmos / DocumentDB billing model is RU-based or serverless.)

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Data-plane (MongoDB protocol) normally uses username/password credentials (SCRAM); for Cosmos DB the username is often <user>@<account> and the password is the primary key or a user password. Management operations use Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) credentials via Azure RBAC. Direct MongoDB driver authentication via Microsoft Entra ID is not the usual path for data-plane reads/writes; the driver uses the connection string with user/password/primary key. (If Azure AD authentication for the MongoDB API exists it is a special preview feature and requires specific token-exchange steps rather than a standard SCRAM URI.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers for application data access (for Python use pymongo or motor). There is no separate data-plane 'DocumentDB' driver for Mongo workloads — use the MongoDB-compatible driver. For management (create account, keys, indexes via Azure) use azure-mgmt-cosmosdb / az CLI.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: On MongoDB 7-style vector support the index is a knnVector index; methods include HNSW (common) and other methods (IVF/DiskANN in some deployments). Example createIndex (Mongo shell / pymongo): db.sanctions.createIndex({embedding: "knnVector"}, {knnVector: {dimensions: 1536, method: "hnsw", M: 16, efConstruction: 200}}).

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Use MongoDB text indexes ($text) or regex queries for lexical matching; vector search is performed via the vector index (knn). Hybrid search is implemented in the application by combining results from a vector similarity query (top-N from knn) and a text/regex/$text query, then merging/scoring results in application logic. There is no single built-in unified "vector + text" operator in Cosmos' MongoDB API (unlike Atlas Search) unless the service exposes a specialized search integration.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Supported server/wire versions depend on the account configuration; modern managed MongoDB-compatible DocumentDB/Cosmos accounts can present MongoDB 6.0/7.0 wire protocol compatibility if chosen at account creation. However, some MongoDB server features may be missing or limited (server-side JavaScript, certain admin commands, some aggregation pipeline stages or storage-engine specific features). Expect subtle behavioral differences because the service translates Mongo protocol to the underlying engine.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: For local development run a standard MongoDB Docker image (e.g. mongo:7.0) and use port 27017: docker run --rm -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -e MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME=dev -e MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD=dev mongo:7.0. Note: the Azure Cosmos DB emulator historically supports the Core (SQL) API and may not fully emulate the MongoDB API; when the emulator lacks the Mongo API use local MongoDB instead and test against the live cluster for service-specific features like vector indexes.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams are a MongoDB feature and are supported only when the service exposes a replica-set style topology that implements the necessary oplog semantics. On managed DocumentDB/Cosmos Mongo API accounts change streams may be supported for certain compatibility versions but might need to be enabled or the account configured appropriately; if unsupported you'll need to poll or use service-specific change capture tools. (I would treat change streams as "possibly supported, check account settings".)

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (the environment mentions a documentdb MCP server named 'documentdb'). The general Azure MCP server does not provide MongoDB data-plane tooling; use the documentdb-specific MCP server for data-plane inspect/index/query tools.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically Microsoft had a service named Azure DocumentDB which evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. "DocumentDB" as a name was the original document store offering and Cosmos DB is the successor umbrella service offering multiple APIs (SQL/Core, MongoDB-compatible, Cassandra-compatible, Gremlin, Table). The open-source 'DocumentDB' project is unrelated; Azure DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is Microsoft's proprietary managed service that exposes a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol for the Mongo API.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: The underlying engine is the Cosmos DB proprietary distributed storage/engine when this is the Azure DocumentDB/Cosmos DB managed service; it implements the MongoDB wire protocol on top. That can change behavior: indexing, consistency, transactions, performance characteristics and some commands differ from a native MongoDB server, so expect subtle compatibility differences even when using standard MongoDB drivers.

answers.question: What index definition does this sample need for vector search?
answers.answer: Create a knnVector index on the embedding field. Example (Mongo shell): db.sanctions.createIndex({embedding: "knnVector"}, {knnVector: {dimensions: 1536, method: "hnsw", M: 16, efConstruction: 200}}). Adjust dimensions to your embedding size.

answers.question: How should the Python app connect to the DocumentDB cluster at runtime?
answers.answer: Read the connection string from environment DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to pymongo. Example: from pymongo import MongoClient; import os; uri = os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']; client = MongoClient(uri, tls=True) — ensure TLS/ssl is enabled and the username/password from the URI are valid for the account.

answers.question: What non-vector indexes does this sample need for regex and text matching?
answers.answer: Create a text index on name and alias fields plus a b-tree index on normalized fields used for regex. Example: db.sanctions.createIndex({name: "text", aliases: "text"}); db.sanctions.createIndex({name_normalized: 1});

answers.question: Which port will the live cluster use and what port should local fallback use in tests?
answers.answer: Azure-managed MongoDB-compatible accounts typically listen on TLS port 10255 (or via SRV with default TLS ports). For local fallback during development use the standard MongoDB port 27017 (e.g. mongo:7.0 Docker image).

answers.question: How will the sample authenticate when run in the developer environment?
answers.answer: For the sample use the connection string credentials (username/password) in DOCUMENTDB_URI; do not attempt Azure AD authentication from the MongoDB driver. Create an account-level or database user in the cluster and embed those credentials in the URI provided at runtime (kept in environment only).
